blocks.title: What the interviewer is really testing
blocks.text: This is **not a CRUD modeling exercise**. Anyone can draw `Movie`, `Theatre`, `Seat`. The interviewer is testing one thing: **can you prevent two users from booking the same seat at the same time without serializing the whole system?** Your entity diagram gets you 10 minutes. Your hold-expiry protocol, lock granularity, and failure handling get you the offer. If you start with getters and setters, you have already lost.
The problem

Design an in-memory movie ticket booking service for a single metro. Users browse movies, pick a show by theatre and time, select specific seats, pay, and get a confirmed ticket. Multiple users compete for the same seats in the same show concurrently. Holds must expire if payment does not complete. A seat must never be sold twice, even under retries, payment failures, and process crashes. You must support search by movie and city, seat map reads, temporary holds, confirmation, and cancellation with refund of the hold.

items: `List<Show> searchShows(movieId, city, date)` — return shows with available seat counts, not full seat maps.
`SeatMap getSeatMap(showId)` — return per-seat status: `AVAILABLE`, `HELD`, `BOOKED` plus price tier.
`Hold holdSeats(userId, showId, List<seatId>)` — atomically hold all seats or none. Returns `holdId` with expiry timestamp. Fails if any seat is not `AVAILABLE`.
`Booking confirmBooking(holdId, paymentToken)` — succeeds only if the hold is live and owned by the caller. Converts `HELD` to `BOOKED`. Must be idempotent.
`cancelBooking(bookingId)` / `expireHold(holdId)` — release seats back to `AVAILABLE`. Cancellation after confirmation triggers refund logic.

blocks.text: Clarify before you code

items.title: Hold then pay, or pay then hold?
items.text: Agree on two-phase: hold for 5-10 minutes, then confirm on payment success. Direct book-on-pay guarantees double-charges and angry retries. State the TTL explicitly and who owns expiry.

items.title: Seat selection model?
items.text: Ask if users pick exact seats or just a count. Exact seats means per-seat contention and atomic multi-seat holds. Count-only is a counter decrement and far easier. Assume exact seats unless told otherwise.

items.title: What is the contention scope?
items.text: Is it one process or many app servers? For LLD, assume single process with many threads, but design the hold table so it can move to a database with a unique constraint later. Name that migration path.

items.title: Payment interaction?
items.text: Is payment synchronous mock or async callback? Agree that `confirmBooking` is called only after payment succeeds, and that payment failure must release the hold. Decide idempotency key source: holdId, not bookingId.

items.title: Cancellation and overbooking?
items.text: Ask if cancellations are allowed, if there are seat categories with different pricing, and if overbooking is ever permitted. Answer is no overbooking. Cancellation just flips state and notifies waitlist if you build one.

blocks.text: Requirements

blocks.caption: Scope agreed before writing any code.
rows: Search shows, view seat map, hold, confirm, cancel
Hold vs confirm split is the core state machine
Atomic multi-seat hold: all or nothing
Without expiry, crashed clients leak inventory forever
No double booking under concurrent holds
Correctness bar; everything else is secondary
High read concurrency on seat maps
Reads outnumber writes 100:1; do not lock reads
Network retries must not create duplicate bookings

blocks.text: Approach 1 — the naive synchronized map

The typical first attempt is a `Map<showId, Map<seatId, Boolean>>` with a single `synchronized book()` method that checks availability and marks booked. It passes a single-threaded demo. It is also exactly what fails in review, because it confuses mutual exclusion with inventory lifecycle. There is no notion of a temporary owner, no expiry, and no separation between intent and commitment. Once you add payment latency inside that synchronized block, throughput collapses and every slow payment blocks every unrelated show.

Why it is not enough: three concrete failures. First, **granularity**: one lock for all shows means a hot blockbuster starves an empty morning show. Throughput drops to one booking at a time. Second, **no TTL**: if the user closes the app after `book` but before payment, the seat is gone forever unless you bolt on a sweeper that cannot distinguish held from booked. Third, **no idempotency or ownership**: a retried request looks like a new request, and any thread can overwrite any reservation. The fix is not a bigger lock. It is a state machine plus a narrow lock.
The real design: per-show lock + hold state machine

Choose this shape: `Show` owns its seats and one `ReentrantLock`. All mutations for that show go through that lock, nothing global. Seats have three states — `AVAILABLE`, `HELD`, `BOOKED` — and `HELD` always carries `holderId` and `expiresAt`. Reads of the seat map are lock-free snapshots. Writes are short critical sections that only flip flags; payment and I/O happen outside the lock. The trade-off you must state: per-show locking gives you serializability per show with full parallelism across shows, at the cost of one lock object per active show. That is cheap and correct. A lock-free CAS per seat looks clever but cannot do atomic multi-seat holds without a two-phase dance, so do not propose it unless asked.

blocks.title: Booking flow
blocks.caption: Hold expires unless confirmed; payment never holds a lock.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  U[User] --> S[Search Shows]
  S --> M[Get SeatMap]
  M --> B[Hold Seats]
  B --> P[Pay Outside Lock]
  P --> C[Confirm Hold]
  C --> T[Ticket Booked]
  B --> E[Expiry Worker]
  E --> R[Release to Available]
  P --> F[Payment Failed]
  F --> R

blocks.text: The flow enforces ordering. `holdSeats` is the only operation that moves `AVAILABLE` to `HELD`, and it does so atomically for the whole seat list or rejects. It returns a `holdId` the client must present to confirm. `confirmBooking` validates ownership and liveness, calls payment verification outside any seat lock in production, then re-enters the show lock briefly to flip `HELD` to `BOOKED`. Expiry is a scheduled task that flips expired `HELD` back to `AVAILABLE`. This is why double-booking disappears: there is exactly one atomic transition out of `AVAILABLE`, guarded by the show lock, and every other path requires proving you own the hold.

blocks.title: Domain model
blocks.caption: Show is the concurrency boundary; Booking is the payment boundary.

blocks.text: Working code

Below is the minimal code that survives concurrency review. Note three decisions: lock lives on `Show`, hold map lives on `Show`, and the scheduler never calls user code while holding the lock. `holdSeats` copies the seat list, validates, then mutates — all inside `tryLock` with timeout so a stuck holder cannot wedge the show forever. `confirm` is idempotent via `holdId` lookup: repeat confirms return the same `Booking` without touching seats. Expiry runs on a background executor and is safe to race with confirm because both re-check state under the same lock.
Complexity

blocks.caption: Costs are per show, not per system.
rows: Index by `movieId+date`; never scan seat maps
Copy under read or volatile read; no lock held for I/O
Background; lock per show briefly, never globally

blocks.text: Concurrency — the hardest follow-up

Expect this prompt: *two users click the same two seats in the same 50ms — prove no double booking.* Walk through it with the lock. Both threads enter `holdSeats` for the same `Show`. Only one acquires the `ReentrantLock`. It validates both seats as `AVAILABLE`, flips them to `HELD` with its `holdId`, and unlocks. The second thread then acquires the lock, sees `HELD` with a live expiry, and returns failure. No database, no distributed lock, no prayer. Explain why alternatives lose: `synchronized` on the service serializes unrelated shows and kills throughput. Per-seat `synchronized` blocks deadlock when two users request seats in opposite order unless you sort seat IDs globally — mention ordered acquisition if you go that route. Optimistic versioning with retry works across servers but adds abort-and-retry complexity the interviewer did not ask for in LLD. For LLD, per-show pessimistic locking is the honest answer: simple, provably correct, and fast enough because the critical section is microseconds and payment stays outside it. Then name the production upgrade: replace the in-memory hold map with a database row per hold plus a unique partial index on `(showId, seatId)` where status is live, so multiple app servers get the same guarantee. The lock becomes a performance optimization; the constraint becomes the correctness backstop.

blocks.title: Never hold a lock across payment
blocks.text: The classic fail is calling the payment gateway while holding the show lock. One slow gateway stalls every buyer for that show and turns a 50ms hold into a 5-second outage. **Validate under lock, pay outside lock, re-validate under lock, then flip.** If payment succeeds but confirm finds the hold expired, refund — do not resurrect the seats.
Follow-ups to have ready

items.title: Support 10 seats together and best-available?
items.text: Keep atomic hold, but add contiguous-seat search: scan rows for a run of AVAILABLE of length k. Trade-off: row-scan is O(seats) per request; cache row availability counters to avoid full scans.

items.title: Different prices and tiers?
items.text: Put price on Seat, not Show. Premium rows cost more. Confirm computes total from seats at hold time and freezes it in the Hold so later price changes do not rewrite a live hold.

items.title: Cancellation and refund?
items.text: Confirm creates a Booking with PENDING then CONFIRMED. Cancel flips BOOKED back to AVAILABLE and emits a refund event. Never delete the Booking row — you need it for idempotency and audit.

items.title: Waitlist for sold-out shows?
items.text: Queue userIds per show. On cancel or expiry, pop and offer a short-lived hold. Trade-off: fairness versus complexity; cap the queue and TTL the offer or you rebuild the same leak.

items.title: Scale to multiple servers?
items.text: Move holds to a database with unique constraint on live seats, use Redis with Lua for fast hold-or-fail, keep per-show lock as in-process fast path. Name the trade-off: latency and ops cost for horizontal scale.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state unprompted

items: Same user retries confirm after timeout — must return same booking, not a second charge; key idempotency on `holdId`.
Hold expires between payment success and confirm — must refund, not confirm; expiry wins.
Partial availability in multi-seat request — reject entire hold, never book a subset silently.
Duplicate seat IDs or empty list in request — validate before locking to avoid poisoning the hold.
Clock skew in expiry — use monotonic clock for TTL checks, wall clock only for display.
Show already started or cancelled — freeze holds; seat map returns read-only.
Two holds for overlapping sets in opposite seat order — per-show single lock removes ordering deadlock entirely.
Sweeper races confirm — both paths re-check `holderId` and status under the same lock; loser aborts cleanly.

blocks.text: How you are graded

blocks.caption: Weak vs strong signals for this round.
rows: Flat `User books Seat` with getters only
Show as aggregate root; Seat, Hold, Booking lifecycles explicit
`synchronized book()` or no lock at all
Per-show lock, short critical section, payment outside lock
TTL + sweeper + idempotent confirm on holdId
Names cost every time: granularity vs complexity vs throughput
Price on seat, state machine supports cancel, waitlist, multi-server constraint

blocks.title: 45-minute plan
blocks.text: Spend it like this: **0-5** clarify hold-vs-book and TTL. **5-12** draw entities and state machine `AVAILABLE → HELD → BOOKED`. **12-28** code `holdSeats` plus `confirm` with per-show lock. **28-38** prove no double booking under 50ms race and explain why payment stays outside the lock. **38-45** handle expiry, idempotent retry, and one follow-up such as cancellation or multi-server constraint. If you are still drawing boxes at minute 20, you are behind.
